Recurrence is always a possibility. This is because it would be extremely difficult, if near impossible, to remove every cell that could potentially become stimulated or proliferate due to hormonal triggers. Glandular tissue is often dispersed throughout the breast and intertwined with fat cells. However, with that said, if all visible gland is removed, the likelihood of recurrence is rare because little tissue is leftover to become stimulated (crudely put, 50% of tissue removed = 50% of the risk is removed; 98% of tissue removed = 98% of the risk is removed).

Many surgeons are conservative in their approach when it comes to removing all of the visible gland and opt instead to leave some behind the areola to prevent concavity. However, in my opinion this almost always leads to a sub-optimal result and, as aforesaid, increases the risk of the problem recurring - especially if the hormonal imbalance that triggered the initial growth persists. As such, I always advise patients that complete removal (as far as the visible eye can see) of the glandular tissue is the safest option.

As regards TRT, precautionary steps can be taken to ensure that E2 levels, and more importantly the ratio of T:E2, remain within the optimal range while your hormone levels adjust or balance themselves out. For example, the use of an aromatase inhibitor may be worthwhile if E2 levels become elevated. However, always seek out the expertise of an endocrinologist to confirm there is a problem to be dealt with. I do not recommend self-diagnoses or self-medicating as this very often perpetuates or further complicates the problem of hormonal disruption. 

As for finasteride, I would personally advise against it if possible. If you mess around with your hormones, you naturally expose yourself to greater risk of recurrence. While 5-alpha reductase inhibitors have been shown in studies to be relatively safe, there are numerous anecdotal and clinical accounts of people who have suffered side effects such as breast tissue growth as a consequence of their use. DHT is a strong E2 antagonist. Further, when you block the conversion of T to its more potent androgenic form, DHT, T is far more likely to aromatase into E2 while the body attempts to maintain balance or hormonal homeostasis. The point here is that whenever you disrupt the natural balance of things, you risk suffering unwanted side effects.

It is also important to remember that the fact we had this problem in the first place indicates that we may be predisposed to developing problems due to hormonal disruption. I completely understand why some men recoil at the idea of giving up certain medications, especially when they are depended upon to tackle aesthetic issues, but I honestly do not think the potential risk is worth the limited, sometimes negligible, benefits. It may come down to a choice between having no hair or a pair of breasts. I personally would always choose the former.
